paras: The lynching of Henry Smith was the killing of a Black man by a mob at Des Arc, Arkansas, in July 1881, after he was accused of raping and murdering a girl of about fourteen. Some thirty or forty men took him from the town jail at night, hanged him, and threw his body into the river. Little Rock dispatches carried the story nationwide within days, and a Memphis paper defended the lynching in an editorial.

According to Little Rock dispatches of July 11, an orphan girl of thirteen or fourteen who lived near Des Arc left for school on a Friday morning and never arrived. Her guardian, named as "Mr. Stallings" or "Mr. Stawlings," raised the alarm when she did not come home, and residents searched through the night. Her body was found on Saturday morning in a corner of a fence beside a bloody, broken fence rail, and the reports said she had been raped and murdered.

The first reports did not agree on a suspect. The Associated Press text said suspicion pointed to "two colored men" who had left the country, while a Chicago Tribune special dispatch blamed an unnamed "negro." A report in the Louisiana Capitolian named "a negro named Joe Rymal" and said about fifty armed and mounted men were searching for him "intending to lynch him when caught"; no later report connects him to Smith.

Henry Smith, described as "colored," was captured and held in the jail at Des Arc after a coroner's inquest. The Memphis Public Ledger added that a constable and a deputy sheriff brought him into town and lodged him there. At about midnight, thirty or forty men took the keys from the jailer, entered the jail and brought Smith out. They hanged him "in the bright moonlight" and threw the body into the river, which the Kennebec Journal identified as the White River. According to the Associated Press account, the men were not masked, and townspeople followed them to the river without anyone trying to stop them.

The same account called the lynching "the coolest and most quiet piece of business imaginable" and said that Smith "confessed his crime," a claim it did not attribute to any witness or official. A one-line brief in the Mineral Point Tribune said he was hanged from a tree, while the fuller accounts do not say what he was hanged from.
No report of an inquest into Smith's death or of arrests among the lynchers appears in the coverage; the Associated Press dispatch closed by saying "popular sympathy" was with them.

On July 12 papers from St. Paul to Washington printed the account of the girl's death, the Wheeling Register under the headline "A Case for Judge Lynch." The same day the Washington Evening Critic already reported Smith's capture and hanging under "Short Work With a Brute." From July 13 the lynching ran in Memphis, Chicago, Wheeling, Omaha, Augusta and Portland, and in Richmond and Savannah the next day. A one-sentence digest version then circulated through weekly papers, among them the Batesville Guard in Arkansas, into early August.

Headlines presented the killing as deserved punishment: "His Just Reward" in Wheeling, "A Negro Brute Lynched" in Savannah, and "The Citizens of Desaro Turn Out and Hang Up a Black Fiend" in the Chicago Tribune. The Associated Press text called the lynchers "avenging angels" and Smith "the monster" and "the fiend," and listed the wounds on the girl's body in detail. The Public Ledger went further, writing that lynching "ought to be prevented" but might be permitted for crimes like this one, and recalling that Des Arc had once tarred and feathered two men who insulted a lady. Shorter items, such as those in the Huntsville Gazette and the Batesville Guard, gave the bare facts without comment but stated the accusation as fact.

The reports conflict on the date of the lynching. The Associated Press placed it at midnight on Saturday, the day the body was found, but the shorter July 12 wire said Smith was "captured yesterday" and hanged "last night." Because the July 11 dispatches still described the suspects as at large, the later date, the night of July 11, fits the sequence of reports better.

The girl was called Lucy Webb in most briefs and Mattie or Matilda Webb in the Associated Press and Public Ledger accounts, and the Evening Critic gave her age as seventeen rather than fourteen. The Omaha Bee placed the murder near Searcy rather than Des Arc. Accounts of her injuries also differ: two dispatches reported a broken neck, while the Associated Press text described a cut throat, stab wounds and a crushed skull.

reader.title: Lynching of Henry Smith
bases: A group of thirty or forty men took Henry Smith from the Des Arc jail, hanged him and threw his body into the river (A8, A19, A6).
Smith was taken from jail by thirty or forty men and hanged without trial on an accusation of rape and murder (A8, A19); every report calls the killers a mob (A6, A7, A11).

Two separately worded Little Rock dispatches (the AP text in A8 and the shorter 'captured yesterday' wire in A6/A7) and the Memphis Public Ledger editorial (A19) agree that a mob took Smith from the Des Arc jail, hanged him and put his body in the river.

accounts.label: AP Little Rock dispatch, July 12
accounts.gist: Smith was lodged in jail after the coroner's inquest; about midnight Saturday thirty or forty unmasked men took the keys, hanged him in the moonlight and cast his body in the river; he had confessed and popular sympathy was with the lynchers.

accounts.label: Short Little Rock wire, July 12
accounts.gist: Smith was captured 'yesterday' (July 11), taken from jail by a mob 'last night', hanged, and his body cut down and thrown into the (White) river.

accounts.label: Memphis Public Ledger editorial
accounts.gist: Repeats the AP account, adds that a constable and deputy sheriff jailed Smith, and argues lynching may be permitted for such a crime.

accounts.label: Early Little Rock reports, July 11
accounts.gist: Before any arrest, suspicion fell on two unnamed colored men who had left, or on 'Joe Rymal', with fifty armed men searching to lynch him.

framing.detail: The AP text calls the lynchers 'avenging angels', Smith 'the monster' and 'the fiend', and says popular sympathy was with the lynchers.
Headlines 'His Just Reward' (Wheeling), 'Short Work With a Brute' (Evening Critic), 'Hang Up a Black Fiend' (Chicago Tribune).
Memphis Public Ledger editorial: lynching 'ought to be prevented' but may be permitted for crimes like this; praises Des Arc's earlier tar-and-feathering.
Weekly digest items give a one-sentence account without comment, though they state the accusation as fact ('the negro who murdered Lucy Webb').

conflicts.note: The July 11 dispatches still describe the suspects as at large and a search under way (A3, A22), which fits the later date; the AP 'Saturday night' would fall on the day the body was found.
